# Introduction

Earlier this year, a very interesting research article came out from a team at
Meta. In this [paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.09871), they propose a new transformers-based architecture for LLMs
which operates at the level of _bytes_ rather than at the level of _tokens_,
thus being dubbed the _Byte Latent Transformer_ (BLT for short 🥪). One
of the central motivations for their proposal is that current tokenization-based
approaches to LLMs are inefficient, in as far as tokenization is a pre-computed
grouping of bytes which doesn't necessarily allocate compute resources
intelligently based on the context. To justify their new architecture, they show
the results from several experiments which shows that their model performs as
well as (or even better in some instances) other frontier models. My goals for
this post is:

* Explain in greater detail the motivation to work on bytes
* Explain the model architecture and how training and inference work.
* Discuss the empirical studies done by the authors as the relate to performance
  and scaling laws for their architecture.
* Raise some questions that I had from reading the paper. 

This post is by no means a substitute for reading the paper, and I highly
encourage you to go do so. However, I hope this post helps in some small way.
And of course, it should go without saying, that any mistakes are mine and mine
alone, and feel free to email me if you have any corrections. 

# LLMs and Tokenization

Before getting into the nitty-gritty of the BLT architecture it seems best to
remind ourselves how LLMs currently work and where this brings up bottlenecks
and pitfalls. <!-- Not sure I love this phrasing -->  Of main concern for the
BLT paper, in particular, is the reliance on tokenization for LLMs. Below is a
diagram which caricatures how LLMs currently work. 

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Input String] --> B[Tokenizer]
  B --> C[Sequence of Tokens]
  C --> D[Decoder-only Transformer]
  D --> E[Probability Distribution]
  E --> F[Next Token]
```

What is the purpose of the tokenizer in the first place? Transformers take in
tensors and output tensors. However, when using a transformer, we want to input
a string of text. The purpose of the tokenizer is to bridge this gap. It takes
in an input string and partitions the string into substrings known as tokens.
These tokens, in turn, are mapped onto integers, and the whole input string is
turned into an array of integers. We can tensorize this array, thereby creating
an object which the transformer can operate on.

There are several tokenizers out there, but all tokenizers use some sort of
algorithm (e.g. Byte Pair Encoding) and a corpus of text to construct the
tokens. Moreover, the tokenizer is trained separately and before any sort of
training takes place for the LLM itself. This means, in particular, that the
tokenizer being used has a _fixed_ token space. In the case of GPT-2 example,
the tokenizer used was trained using the BPE algorithm and has 50,257 tokens. 

After converting an input text into an array of integers, we feed that into
the LLM and get an output tensor which is a probability distribution over the
token space. In the case of GPT-2, then, this would be a 50,257-vector.

Let's go through this diagram step-by-step with a running example using the
GPT-2 tokenizer. Suppose that the input sentence is `"The cat is on the"`. This
is tokenized into the following sequence: `["The", " cat", " is", " on", " the"]`.

These are then turned into a tensor array of integers `[464, 3797, 318, 319, 262]`.
Feeding these into the transformer, we get an output tensor of length 50,257.
Taking the argmax of this probability tensor we are likely to get the integer
2603, which corresponds to the token `" mat"`. Note how the tokenizer determines the type of output the transformer will
output. 

The use of tokenizers come with certain trade-offs. For one, they have a fixed
token space as mentioned earlier. This results in the tokenizer not being able
to recognize sequences of characters which are out of sample. Another, more
subtle problem, is that the tokenizer can change how it tokenizes once later
